title: Moses runs (Exodus 2:11–22)
hook: he kills an Egyptian, flees, and becomes a stranger in a strange land
carry: a stranger in a strange land

segments.voice: Yesterday, tevah: a mother, a sister, a princess, and a baby drawn out of the water. Your line was someone was watching.

Moses grows up in the palace: Egyptian clothes, Egyptian schooling, a princess for a mother. But he knows, somehow, who his people are. One day, a grown man, he goes out and watches them carrying their loads. He sees an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own. Moses looks this way and that way, sees no one, kills the Egyptian, and hides the body in the sand. It's the first thing the adult Moses does in the Bible. Not a miracle. A killing, done in anger, in secret, with a glance over his shoulder.
screen: `RAISED IN THE PALACE.` → `HE SEES THE BEATING.` → `THIS WAY AND THAT WAY.`

segments.voice: The next day he sees two Hebrews fighting, and tells the one in the wrong to stop. The man turns on him, in the King James Bible: "Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?" Are you going to kill me like you killed the Egyptian? So it's known. Pharaoh wants him dead, and Moses runs, east out of Egypt, all the way to the land of Midian, and sits down by a well. Wells keep turning up in this story: Rebekah at one, Jacob and Rachel at another. Seven sisters come to water their father's flock, and shepherds drive them off. Moses stands up for them and waters their flock. At home they tell their father: an Egyptian rescued us. In Egypt he's a Hebrew. In Midian he's an Egyptian. He belongs nowhere. The father takes him in, Moses marries one of the daughters, Zipporah, and they have a son. Moses names him Gershom, saying: "I have been a stranger in a strange land." Ger is the Hebrew word for a stranger, a foreigner living among people not their own. Christians and Jews have both struggled with the killing: was it justice, or rage? In the book of Acts, Stephen retells it as Moses taking his people's side, supposing they would understand that God meant to free them by his hand; they didn't. The Bible doesn't settle it. But it never forgets what Moses learned in Midian. Israel's law will later say: don't oppress a stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.
screen: `WHO MADE THEE A JUDGE OVER US?` · `HE RUNS TO MIDIAN.` · `AN EGYPTIAN RESCUED US.` · `GER: A STRANGER.` · then, large: `I HAVE BEEN A STRANGER IN A STRANGE LAND.`

segments.voice: Remember a time you were the stranger, a new school, a new job, a new country, a room where you knew no one, and who helped. Now think of someone around you who is new right now, a neighbor, a coworker, a family at school, and picture greeting them. If you pray, you can pray for them.
Moses runs. After killing an Egyptian, he flees to Midian, marries, and names his son for what he has become: a stranger in a strange land.
Your line: a stranger in a strange land. Moses knew that edge well. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians often draw on Moses's years as a stranger in Midian, and on the laws about strangers that follow from Israel's time in Egypt, when churches welcome immigrants and refugees.

what it means: he begins with a killing, is rejected by his own people, flees, and becomes a stranger far from home.
what a scholar hears: Gershom is explained by ger, stranger; the Torah repeatedly tells Israel to protect the ger because they were strangers in Egypt.

chat.says: Wait, Moses killed someone? Why did he end up in Midian?
options: He killed an Egyptian beating a Hebrew; when it got out, he fled and lived there as a stranger.
Pharaoh's daughter sent him to Midian to find a wife among her own people.
He was exiled for refusing to bow to Pharaoh's gods, and Midian took him in.
chat.meaning: When the killing became known, Pharaoh wanted him dead. Moses fled to Midian, married Zipporah, and named his son for being a stranger.

Midian.meaning: the land Moses fled to, where he married

Zipporah.meaning: Moses's wife, one of seven sisters at the well

Gershom.meaning: Moses's son, named for being a stranger

Ger.meaning: Hebrew for a stranger living among another people

Stephen.meaning: an early Christian in Acts who retells Moses's story

notes: The father is called Reuel in 2:18 and Jethro in 3:1; the script avoids naming him.
Stephen's retelling (Acts 7:23–29) summarized as Moses 'defending his people too soon'; Stephen says Moses supposed his brethren would understand. Confirm the paraphrase is fair.
'Moses runs east': Midian is generally placed east of Egypt (northwest Arabia / Sinai); confirm or drop 'east'.

Audit (10% sample): Acts 7 paraphrase 'defending his people too soon' was not Stephen's framing; now follows Acts 7:24–25 (he supposed his brethren would understand that God would deliver them by his hand, but they understood not).
